# The update-docs process

Reflect a **finalized** code change in documentation. Run after the work is done, not during it.

The docs root is the directory holding `.doc-marshal.toml`; `doc-marshal doctor` names it. The
rules live in the tool and win on any conflict with this file:

- `doc-marshal info --rules` -- every rule `check` enforces that is not per-type: notes,
  attachments, naming, frontmatter and anchors, the index, links, numbered notes, structure,
  nomenclature notes. Read it in Stage 4, before writing.
- `doc-marshal info` and `doc-marshal info <type>` -- the types: what each serves, its voice,
  structure, mutability and frontmatter. Read them in Stage 2, when routing.

## Non-goals -- read first

This process **maintains a convention on the docs a change touched**. Its scope is the change, not
the tree. On every run:

- Touch only docs the change actually affects. Never sweep the docs root.
- Do **not** open a doc to tidy it. A doc enters scope because the change made it wrong or incomplete.
- Do **not** reorganize folders. Moving a doc rewrites paths for every doc that links to it, which
  drags docs outside your scope into the run.
- Do **not** mine existing docs for retroactive `decision` records.

Something wrong outside the change's scope is not yours to fix on this run. Name it in the report and
leave it.

## Scope

Which surfaces you may touch at all. What a note must satisfy is the rules; how to write one, and
the approval gates, are Stage 4.

| Surface | May you touch it |
| --- | --- |
| notes under the docs root | yes -- create, edit, propose deletion. Renaming is in scope but gated: Stage 4 |
| `INDEX.md` | never by hand -- generated output. Stage 5 regenerates it with `doc-marshal index` |
| `assets/**` | no -- attachments, exempt from validation, names not yours |
| `NOMENCLATURE.md`, at any level | read it, write by it -- editing the vocabulary is its own task, not part of a docs run |
| agent-memory files (`CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`) | yes, surgically -- Stage 4 says how narrowly |
| docstrings and comments in the project's source | yes -- but only in the files the change touched, which Stage 1's diff already gave you |
| any other documentation tree | no -- see below |

**One** documentation tree is in scope. Every other documentation surface -- a published site, a
wiki export, generated API docs -- is out of bounds: do not read it, write it, or link into it. If the
change clearly falsified something there, name it in the report and leave it. An agent-memory file
that says what a tree is for overrides this in either direction. Check once, in Stage 1, and say in
the plan gate what you concluded.

## Stage 1 -- Scope the change

The user's invoking message is the **primary** determinant of what to document. Git fills the gaps.

1. Take the change description from the invocation and from the session, if the work happened here.
2. Fill gaps with git. Changes routinely span several commits, so work from a range:

   ```bash
   range=$(doc-marshal affected --print-range)   # empty on the trunk

   git log --oneline $range     # shape of the branch
   git diff --stat $range       # what it touched
   git diff $range -- <path>    # the parts that matter
   ```

   The tool resolves the trunk and computes the merge-base, so the range never picks up trunk
   commits made since the branch point -- do not hand-write `trunk..HEAD`, which does. Add
   `git status` when uncommitted work is in play.
3. Read the code that changed. You need the current state, not just the diff.
4. Ask the anchors which notes the change reaches:

   ```bash
   doc-marshal affected    # branch commits + uncommitted work
   ```

   This matches every note's repo-path anchors against the changed paths -- exactly the question
   "which docs does this diff touch?". Do not hand-read frontmatter to answer it.

   Its output is a starting set, not the answer, in both directions. A note whose subject the change
   affects **without** touching a path it names will not appear, so also grep the docs root for
   changed symbols, config keys and public identifiers. And a note that appears is not automatically
   in scope -- the change may not have touched the part of the code it describes.

An empty range means you are on the trunk. Do not widen it by guessing a commit count: use
`git log --oneline -10` and `git status`, state which commits you are treating as the change, and
confirm before writing.

**If you cannot name a concrete change set -- specific commits or paths, from the invocation, the
session, or the diff -- stop and ask what changed.** A run with no change set has nothing to
document, and "the docs are out of date" is not a change set. This holds in auto mode.

Then present, as one confirmable summary:

- **Change set**: the commits/paths in scope, in one or two lines.
- **Doc targets**: each doc you propose to touch, its type, the action (edit / create /
  delete-proposal), and a one-clause reason. If no doc needs to change, say so -- a run that
  documents nothing is a valid outcome, not a failure to find work.
- **Anything you are unsure is in scope**, called out explicitly.

Ask when the change set is ambiguous, spans subsystems you did not expect, or names a change you
cannot locate in the code. Otherwise present the summary as prose and continue -- do not stall on an
obvious scope.

## Stage 2 -- Route each need to a type

Run `doc-marshal info` for the enabled types and `doc-marshal info <type>` for the argument behind
each. With the standard preset, route by what the reader needs:

| The change introduces | Type |
| --- | --- |
| a config field, an event code, a schema, a CLI surface -- a fact this repo **decides** | `reference`, anchored with `code_refs` |
| a part's specs, a measurement, a vendor protocol, third-party behaviour -- a fact it **observes** | `reference`, anchored with `source` (and `code_refs` where we implement against it) |
| a procedure to run: a deploy, a validation, a setup, a recovery | `runbook` |
| how an application or feature behaves **as a whole**, at any stage from proposed to built | `spec` -- and a change to built behaviour updates the existing spec's body and `status` |
| a choice with live alternatives that is likely to be revisited | `decision` |
| a term the project uses inconsistently, or a word that needs ruling out | `nomenclature` -- but see the vocabulary rule in Stage 4: not on this run |

Two rules govern the routing itself:

- **One type per document.** A change needing both a procedure and its rationale is two docs linked
  to each other, not one mixed doc.
- **Prefer editing an existing doc.** A new note is justified when no existing doc owns the subject,
  not when the subject is new to you.

`reference` vs `spec` turns on **scope**, not on time. A spec says what a feature does end to end
and links to the references that hold the facts it rests on; a reference holds one granular subject.
Rationale for a choice with live alternatives is a `decision`; rationale that helps a reader use a
fact stays in the reference that states it. A dead end with no choice behind it goes in the commit
message, not in a note.

A `spec` whose code the change touched is rewritten to match and stays `done`. A spec the change
rewrote *ahead* of the code goes to `in-progress`; the validator warns when a `done` spec was
edited by a change that touched none of its `code_refs`, and that warning is the prompt to decide.

## Stage 3 -- Plan gate

**Default: stop here and wait.** Present the plan as a table -- doc path, type, action, one-clause
reason -- and get approval before writing anything.

**In auto mode:** skip the gate for edits and creations, then report what you did. Auto mode
suppresses *this* gate only. Renames, new agent-memory sections, and deletion proposals still require
approval -- present those and wait, auto or not.

A plan naming more than about six docs is a signal you have mis-scoped, not a large run. Stop and
confirm the change set before writing, auto or not.

## Stage 4 -- Write

**Read `doc-marshal info --rules` now, before writing.** Do not work from memory of it, and do not
restate its rules inside a doc.

### Vocabulary rule

Write in the terms the docs root's `NOMENCLATURE.md` defines, and in the terms of any `NOMENCLATURE.md` in a
directory above the note you are writing. Where it rules a word out, use the term it names instead.
Where a word is in backticks because it is the literal name of a field, a flag or an API, leave it
alone -- that is what the backticks are for.

**Do not edit `NOMENCLATURE.md` as part of a docs run.** If the change needs a term the vocabulary does
not have, or contradicts one it does, write the docs in the existing terms and say so in the Stage 6
report. Changing what a word means is a decision about the domain, not a documentation update, and
it lands as its own task.

### Evidence rule

Every factual claim must be traceable to the **code or config** you read in this session. If you
cannot point at the line that makes a statement true, do not write the statement. Another doc is not
evidence -- it may be the thing that drifted. Never document from memory or inference; that is how
confident-sounding drift gets in.

### Style

- Sentence case in headings; the H1 is the human title. Imperative mood in instructions.
- Link inline, on first mention of a concept that has its own note, once per section. A note does
  not end with a list of its neighbours.
- Describe a value by its role and name the file that owns it -- "once per `worker.poll_interval`" --
  rather than embedding the number. Runbooks are the exception: an operator needs a literal command.
- Say what is true and what is not yet true; where the docs distinguish implemented from running in
  production, keep the distinction.
- A fact that came from outside the repository carries a `source` anchor, on any type, beside any
  `code_refs` for the code that implements it.

### Creating a note

Scaffold it rather than typing frontmatter from memory. The path is read from the current
directory, so run this from the repository root:

```bash
doc-marshal new <type> <docs root>/<folder>/<slug>.md --summary "<one line>" --code-ref <path>
doc-marshal new decision <slug> --summary "<one line>"
```

It applies the mechanical part of the rules -- today's date, the fields the type requires, a
numbered note's number, location and title prefix, a nomenclature note's filename, and every
section the type requires. It does not validate: the scaffold fails `doc-marshal check` until its
required sections are written, and the `next:` line it prints is the gate. The required sections
are the note's spine; any heading beyond them earns its place or is deleted.

### Renaming

Rename only when a note's subject has become something else. When it is, do it as one complete
operation:

1. `git mv <old path> <new path>` -- always `git mv`, so history follows the file.
2. Find every inbound reference rather than assuming there are none: `git grep -In "old-name"`. That
   covers every tracked file, so notes, code comments, CI config and agent-memory pointers all
   surface; untracked work in progress will not, so check `git status` if that is in play.
3. Repair each one: links in other notes, `See <docs root>/...` pointers in code, and any path
   referenced from an agent-memory file.
4. Re-grep for the old name. A rename that leaves a dangling reference is a failed rename.

Renames need approval even in auto mode -- they are the most disruptive thing this process does.
Attachments under `assets/` are out of scope (Scope), so a docs run never renames one.

### Agent-memory files (`CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`)

Edit **only where the change falsified an existing assertion.** These files are dense curated prose
on a shared context budget; do not append material because it is interesting. Some projects keep one
at the root, some one per directory -- edit the nearest one making the falsified claim, and none
other.

- A statement the change made wrong gets a surgical edit.
- A pointer into the docs root whose target moved or whose claim changed gets fixed. The root
  `CLAUDE.md` may carry an `@<docs root>/CLAUDE.md` import line that `doc-marshal init` wrote; it
  is what puts the docs-root pointer in every session, so it stays.
- A **genuinely new subsystem** gets a proposed new paragraph or section -- present it for approval,
  do not write it silently. This applies even in auto mode.
- **Never hand-write an index**, here or anywhere: no tree, folder listing or "contents of this
  directory" section. A committed listing's only job is to agree with the filesystem, and it stops
  doing that silently. The one index is generated (`doc-marshal info --rules` §5).

### In-code docs

- Fix docstrings and comments the change made wrong.
- **Delete** comments the change made obsolete -- a comment describing a workaround that no longer
  exists is worse than none.
- Add a docstring to genuinely new public API: what it does and how to use it. Rationale and
  alternatives go in the docs root, linked with a `See <docs root>/...` reference.
- Keep `See <docs root>/...` pointers valid when notes are created, renamed or moved.

### Obsolete docs

When the change made a doc wrong in a way editing cannot fix, **propose deletion; never delete.**
List each candidate with the reason it is now wrong and what supersedes it, and let the user decide.
This holds in auto mode too.

## Stage 5 -- Verify

All three steps run before you report done.

1. **Validator** -- `doc-marshal check <the files you touched>`.

   A write-time hook may already have run this on each note as you wrote it, so this should be
   clean. Run it anyway: the hook sees one file at a time and misses what only the finished set
   shows -- a rename's inbound links, a number collision, a link into a note written later in the run.

   It enforces the rules, so a surprising result means reading the rule rather than working around
   the tool. A clean run says the note's shape is right, not that its content is: the evidence rule
   and the style below are yours to hold.

   **Pass the files you touched and nothing else, and fix what it reports on those files.** Anything
   it reports about a doc outside your change set falls under Non-goals: name it in the report and
   leave it. Do not edit a doc you did not touch to make this step pass. If you scope the run with
   `--range`, it is `A..B` -- two commits, two dots -- or the command refuses it.

2. **Fresh-reader test** -- for new notes and substantially rewritten ones; skip it when the run
   only made small edits to existing prose. Launch a read-only subagent with no session context.
   Give it the paths you wrote and 4-6 questions a real reader would bring, and ask it to answer
   from the docs alone and report what was ambiguous, what knowledge the docs assumed, and any
   internal contradiction. Fix what it surfaces; re-run only if you made substantive changes.

3. **Index** -- `doc-marshal index`, whenever the run created, renamed or deleted a note, or changed
   a `type` or `summary`. Skip it when the run only edited prose inside existing notes.

   `INDEX.md` is the tree's only routing surface, so a run that changes the note set and leaves the
   index behind hands the next reader a map that no longer matches the tree.

   Regeneration is whole-tree, so it can fail on a note you never opened -- the builder names the
   offender and writes nothing. That note is not yours to fix (Non-goals): name it in the report and
   leave the index stale. The pre-commit hook and CI both check it again.

## Stage 6 -- Report

A chat summary only -- no run log, no changelog note. The git diff is the record; if the docs root is
a separate repo or submodule, say so, because the change then spans two commits. Report:

- Each doc touched, with its type and a one-line description of what changed.
- Every rename, as `old -> new`, with the count of inbound references you repaired.
- Deletion proposals awaiting the user's decision.
- Anything you deliberately did **not** document, and why -- including anything the validator
  reported outside your change set.
- Whether you regenerated `INDEX.md`, or which note outside your change set blocked the rebuild.
- What the reader test surfaced and how you resolved it, or that the run did not warrant one.

Then recommend a read-through: the user owns these docs.
